I host a dinner for eight about once a month, and I have one rule: the first twenty minutes are mine. People arrive a little nervous, even people who know each other, and somebody has to break the ice for them. So I introduce every guest with one fact that invites a question. This is Ana, she has just come back from Japan. And now Ana has something to say, and the person next to her has something to ask. After that, my job gets quieter. I watch for the lull, because there is always one, usually just after the main course arrives. And I watch for the guest who has not said anything for ten minutes. You do not ask that person a big question. You ask a small one with a tag at the end, something they can simply agree with. You grew up by the sea, didn't you? It sounds like nothing. It is an open door, and nine times out of ten they walk through it.

When I moved to London from Lisbon, my English was good, and for the whole first year people found me slightly cold. It took a colleague to explain why. I asked questions like a lawyer. Is the meeting at three? Did you read the report? Perfectly correct, and completely flat. The people around me were doing something else. The meeting is at three, isn't it? You read the report, didn't you? The tag turns a demand into an invitation. And there are really two tags hiding in the same words. If my voice goes down at the end, I am not asking anything. I am inviting you to agree, which is what you do at a dinner table. If it goes up, I genuinely do not know the answer, which is what you do in a meeting when the answer matters. The words are identical. Only the tune changes, and the tune is what people remember about you.
